label: Figure 1
title: The drive to outcome chain, with the nominal and effective stimulus at the coupling join
caption: The seven levels this volume uses to write any modality as one chain: drive, coupling, cellular, subcellular/molecular, circuit, system, outcome. The nominal and effective stimulus are drawn as a separate pair at the drive/coupling join, because what the operator set and what reached the tissue can differ in magnitude and, for drugs, in identity. Two joins are marked as the weakest: biophysics to molecules, where the transducing cell and molecule are often unknown, and animal mechanism to human outcome, where a trial often cannot show whether the mechanism was engaged at all. The loop back from system to circuit is there because a reflex has to be drawn as a cycle rather than a line.
how_to_read: Read the solid arrows left to right as one pass from what is delivered to what is measured. Each arrow is a place where a separate measurement or model is needed, not a step that follows automatically from the one before it. Start at the drive, then look at the nominal/effective pair: if a study reports only the nominal stimulus, everything downstream rests on an inference. The two arrows marked as weakest joins are where this literature most often breaks, so when you read a claim that spans one of them, ask what was measured on each side and in which species. Follow the feedback arrow if the system you are reading about regulates itself, as the vagal immune loop does.
source: Built from section 2 of the review. No cited paper states this seven-step chain; it is assembled by this volume from the brain-stimulation chain of induced field to local and network effects to behaviour [199] and the drug-development chain of exposure, target binding and pharmacological activity [24], with the levels-of-organisation commitment from [6] and its limits from [5,8]. The worked example along the chain is the vagal route to immune control [149]. The claim that these two joins are the weakest is the Atlas's reading across the corpus, not a statement any one source makes. Nothing in the figure is quantitative, so nothing in it is approximate; the node ordering is a conceptual scheme, not a measured sequence.

label: Figure 2
title: What counts as dose in each drive class, and what is missing
caption: Eight drive classes set side by side on three questions: which quantities the literature reports, which of them are standardised, and which are missing. No class reduces to a single intensity, and no two classes report the same kind of quantity. ECT and MST are kept as separate rows, as section 3 keeps them, because their dose traditions and their open questions differ.
how_to_read: Pick a drive class and read across the three columns. The middle column tells you what you can expect any competent paper in that family to report; the right-hand column tells you what you will not find even in a good one. Treat the right-hand column as this volume's reading of the cited sources rather than as a claim any single source makes. The numbers in brackets are reference numbers, so you can check each cell against its source.

label: Figure 3
title: Field strengths and thresholds, measured and modelled, on a log scale
caption: Nine field quantities in volts per metre, on a log axis, so measured human intracranial fields, rodent thresholds and modelled temporal-interference thresholds can be seen against one another. The two measured human values sit near or below the rodent threshold for changing spiking, and the modelled temporal-interference threshold sits about two orders of magnitude above the field a tolerable scalp current delivers. 1 mV/mm equals 1 V/m; values reported in mV/mm have been written in V/m without other conversion.
how_to_read: Read each bar as one quantity with its unit, not as a comparison of like with like. Check the "measured or modelled" column before you compare two bars: a measured field in a patient and a threshold from a neuron model are different kinds of number. Check the species column too, because the rodent threshold and the human delivered field come from different preparations. The axis is logarithmic, so equal spacing means equal ratio, and the gap between the delivered field and the modelled temporal-interference threshold is a factor of roughly a hundred, not a small step. Ranges are drawn as bars from the low to the high value as the source reports them.
source: Values transcribed from sections 3.2, 4.2, 4.3 and 4.6 of the review, each row keeping its source, its species and whether it was measured or modelled. Unit harmonisation is the only arithmetic: mV/mm is written as V/m, which is an identity, not an approximation. The values are themselves approximate as their sources report them (about 0.8 V/m, about 0.5 mV/mm, about 1 mV/mm, ranges of 0.1-1, 17-47, 75-230 V/m). The ferret row is an endogenous field measured during physiological activity, included as a reference point rather than as a stimulation quantity, and it is neither human nor rodent. No two rows were produced by the same procedure, so the figure compares literatures, not measurements.

label: Figure 4
title: Coupling mechanisms and their named rivals, by drive
caption: Six drives, each joined to the transducer its literature proposes as primary and to the rival accounts that explain the same observations. Pressure has the most crowded set: mechanosensitive channels, the lipid bilayer itself, acoustic radiation force, astrocytic TRPA1, and the auditory pathway as a confound that competes with all of them. Light and ligand have rivals that are not other transducers at all: too little light arriving, and a metabolite rather than the injected compound doing the binding. Each edge is labelled with the preparation the evidence comes from.
how_to_read: Start at a drive node on the left and follow its edges. The edge labelled as proposed primary is the account its own literature puts first; the edges labelled as rivals are the named competitors, not weaker versions of the same idea. Read the preparation on each edge before you weigh two edges against each other: a computational model, an oocyte, an ex vivo retina and a human volunteer are not interchangeable evidence. Where a drive has several rivals, take them as unresolved rather than ranked, because the section they come from does not choose between them.
source: Built from section 5 of the review, with the electrical case left to section 4. Nothing in the figure is quantitative. The corpus contains no study identifying the transducer in human tissue for ultrasound, so every pressure edge is animal, in vitro or computational.

label: Figure 5
title: Convergence map: modalities and the molecular endpoints they are said to meet at
caption: Eleven modalities on one side and five shared molecular endpoints on the other: BDNF and TrkB, mTOR, immediate-early genes, mitochondrial and metabolic state, and glial and inflammatory signalling. Every edge carries the kind of evidence it rests on and the species it was measured in. Several edges are marked contested, and two are marked as resting on one laboratory. The map shows a shared vocabulary rather than a shared mechanism: a marker that rises by two different routes gives two different edges with the same head node.
how_to_read: Read an edge as "this drive was reported to change this endpoint, in this preparation, by this kind of study" - not as "these drives work the same way". Before joining two edges into a convergence, check that they carry the same assay and the same species; if they do not, the join is weaker than it looks. Pay attention to the flags: contested edges have a published counter-result, single-laboratory edges have no independent replication in this corpus, and the TSPO edge is a null obtained with a marker that does not index activation in primates. Where an edge points at BDNF and TrkB, read the node's own note first, because that one name covers four different kinds of measurement.
source: Built from section 7 of the review only, and restricted to the endpoints and edges that section states. No convergence is asserted that the prose does not: where the section says a marker is shared but the mechanism is not, the edges are kept separate and flagged rather than merged. The strongest form of convergence evidence named in that section - four unrelated compounds abolished by the same NMDA receptor pretreatment in mice - is carried as a property of the contested ketamine edge rather than as a node, because the section presents it as a shared requirement, not a sixth endpoint. Nothing is quantitative and nothing is approximated; the arrangement of modalities against endpoints is this volume's.

label: Figure 6
title: The modality map: 36 families on eight shared axes

columns.label: Spatial and temporal resolution as reported

caption: Thirty-six human-applicable families on eight shared axes. Cells that in the review read only "not established in this corpus" are left empty here, so the gaps are visible as gaps: they cluster in the named-rival column and in proposed primary coupling, while the evidence-base column has none. Reading down the columns rather than across the rows shows that invasiveness does not track how well the coupling step is specified.
how_to_read: Read one row to see what a family's own literature says about itself, and read one column to compare that claim across families. Treat an empty cell as "no source available to this section reports it", not as zero and not as an absence in the world. Do not compare two spatial or temporal figures directly: the TMS numbers are simulations, the tES field values are intracranial recordings, and ultrasound exposure is reported twice, as free-field output and as an in situ estimate. The reference numbers in each cell and in the sources column let you take any claim back to its paper.
source: A transcription of the comparison table in section 10 of the review: 36 rows and eight content columns, cell text as written there, with the citations kept inside the cells. The only change is that 21 cells whose entire content was the placeholder "not established in this corpus" are stored as empty values so that missing data is machine-visible; cells that qualify the placeholder with anything further are kept in full. The ref column is assembled by this figure from the reference numbers appearing anywhere in the row, so it is a row-level index rather than a per-cell citation. Every figure in the table is as reported by that family's own literature, in its own preparation and units, and no two were produced by the same procedure, so the table is a map of what each literature says about itself rather than a measurement of the families against one another.

rows.drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulses across an electrode–tissue interface, Faradaic and non-Faradaic charge transfer [63]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Axonal excitation; driving term is the second spatial derivative of extracellular potential along the fibre (computational) [33]; axons before somata, polarity- and orientation-dependent [34]
rows.named_rival: Informational lesion: high-frequency stimulation makes output regular and variance-free, so the nucleus fires but stops transmitting information (computational) [133]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, train timing; safety bounded jointly by charge density and charge per phase, ~10–800 µC/cm² and 0.05–5 µC/phase, cat cortex [16], fitted as a log-linear limit [17]; effective dose often omitted [2]
rows.resolution_reported: Effective spatial unit is the connected fibre set: structural and functional connectivity independently predicted motor gain in 51 patients and replicated in a second cohort [132]; chronaxie ~50–100 µs for central myelinated axons, 200–700 µs in grey matter [34]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human clinical cohorts [132]; cat cortex damage data [16]; computational axon models [33,133]
rows.what_is_missing: Routine effective-dose reporting [2]; frequency, duty cycle, current density and electrode size in the safety rule [18]; adjudication of excitation versus informational lesion [133]

rows.drive_physically: Same pulses, delivered only while a subthalamic beta-band local field potential burst exceeds threshold [135]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: As open-loop DBS [33]; the biomarker gates delivery rather than altering coupling [135]
rows.named_rival: Not established in this corpus; random intermittent stimulation did not match adaptive stimulation, so timing rather than intermittency carried the benefit [135]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Gating threshold plus the underlying pulse parameters; blinded motor scores improved 50%, about 27% better than continuous stimulation, with total stimulation time down 56% [135]
rows.resolution_reported: Temporal resolution set by the burst detector; spatial as open-loop DBS [135]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human, 8 patients with advanced Parkinson's disease, within-subject blinded comparison [135]
rows.what_is_missing: What "dose" denotes when delivery is state-gated [135]; long-term controlled trials, not established in this corpus

rows.invasiveness: Transcranial drive that deliberately induces a generalised seizure, with cognitive adverse effects as its limiting cost [263]
rows.drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulse trains through scalp electrodes, with placement, pulse amplitude, shape and width, and train frequency, directionality, polarity and duration as separate physical variables [261]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Contested at the level of the drive itself: the antidepressant action is attributed to the induced seizure, to the electrical stimulation, or to their interaction, and the mechanism review that poses the question leaves it open [263]
rows.named_rival: The seizure account against the direct-field account [263]; simulation puts ECT's suprathreshold volume well above that of magnetic seizure therapy, so comparable efficacy from a much more focal field favours the seizure [225,227]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Placement and pulse width are the decisive axes: ultrabrief 0.3 ms right unilateral gave 73% remission against 35% for ultrabrief bilateral in a 2 × 2 randomised design in 90 patients, so efficacy does not follow delivered charge [260]; total charge and energy are argued to be the wrong abstraction [261]; in macaque, seizure threshold was lowest near 16 pulses per second across 5–240 pulses per second and 230–565 mA [226]; three sessions weekly for three weeks [170], median six sessions to remission [171]
rows.resolution_reported: Larger suprathreshold brain volume than MST in finite-element simulation of four ECT montages against three MST coils [225]; seizure induction immediate, course over weeks [260]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: meta-analysis in which real ECT beat simulated (sham) ECT and pharmacotherapy, with bilateral placement and higher dose better than unilateral and lower dose on efficacy [262]; randomised parameter trial, n = 90 [260]; two open-label head-to-heads against intravenous ketamine, response 41.2% versus 55.4% [170] and remission 63% versus 46% [171]; macaque threshold mapping [226]
rows.what_is_missing: Whether the seizure or the field carries the effect [263]; a dosing abstraction better than charge or multiples of seizure threshold [261]; clinical frequencies sit far above the charge-minimising optimum measured in macaque [226]

rows.invasiveness: Transcranial magnetic drive that deliberately induces a generalised seizure, with fewer cognitive adverse effects than ECT in a blinded head-to-head [227]
rows.drive_physically: High-intensity, high-frequency magnetic pulse trains inducing an eddy current confined largely to superficial cortex [225]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Seizure induction from a focal induced field, which reaches a smaller suprathreshold brain volume than any ECT montage at comparable clinical effect [225,227]
rows.named_rival: As for ECT, the seizure against the field: comparable efficacy from a much more focal field is the main argument for the seizure account [227,263]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Coil design, train frequency and stimulator output: in macaque, thresholds were mapped across 5–100 pulses per second at 66–86% of maximum stimulator output, with the fewest pulses needed at mid-range frequencies [226]; field magnitude and suprathreshold volume from simulation [225]
rows.resolution_reported: Field confined much more to superficial cortex than four ECT electrode configurations, in a finite-element comparison [225]; MST required more treatment sessions than ECT [227]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: one double-blind randomised trial at three hospitals in 73 adults — response 51.4% for MST against 42.1% for ultrabrief right unilateral ECT, sustained at six months, with significantly longer time to reorientation and fewer cognitive adverse effects [227]; macaque threshold mapping [226]; simulation [225]
rows.what_is_missing: Which train parameters set the human seizure threshold [226]; any trial beyond the single blinded head-to-head [227]

rows.invasiveness: Implanted extradural electrode; not established in this corpus as a therapy [30,31]
rows.drive_physically: Not established in this corpus; the corpus's epidural material is recordings, not therapeutic drive [58]

rows.family: TMS, theta burst and accelerated protocols

rows.proposed_primary_coupling: As single-pulse TMS, at axon terminals [41]; after-effects read as LTP/LTD-like plasticity [38]
rows.named_rival: Which interneuron network a pulse recruits, indexed by anterior–posterior-current MEP latency, rather than plasticity capacity, explains responder status [59]

rows.drive_physically: Sustained low-intensity current applied at the scalp [43]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Compartment-specific membrane polarisation: about 0.12 mV per mV/mm at the soma along the somato-dendritic axis, largest at dendritic tips, with no clear threshold (rat hippocampal slice) [36]; morphology-dependent, layer V pyramidal cells most sensitive (rat, in vitro) [49]

rows.resolution_reported: Polarisation time constants about 15–70 ms, with excitability changes outlasting the field by more than a second, rat slice [36]; field strength changed little with region or frequency in human and macaque recordings [211]; no focality figure in this corpus
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Rat slice and in vitro [36,49]; human intracranial measurement [40,211]; pooled human safety data [43]
rows.what_is_missing: Whether 1–2 mA modulates neurons directly [36,50]; a consensus in-tissue metric [14]

rows.drive_physically: Sinusoidal current applied at the scalp [43]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Spike-timing entrainment without rate change, dose-dependent at human-feasible intensities in awake macaque [51,52]; network resonance amplifies weak fields, largest when stimulation matches the intrinsic rhythm (ferret slice plus simulation) [37,53]
rows.named_rival: Transcutaneous stimulation of peripheral nerves: anaesthetising the skin reduced tremor entrainment and peripheral stimulation alone reproduced the motor effects (rat and human) [54]; countered by entrainment persisting under topical anaesthesia in macaque [55]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Same envelope as tDCS, to 4 mA and 60 min/day [43]; frequency relative to the intrinsic rhythm [53]; endogenous fields for comparison were 2–4 mV/mm in ferret cortex [37]
rows.resolution_reported: Phase locking altered without firing-rate change, including in macaque hippocampus and basal ganglia [51]; entrainment competes with ongoing oscillations and can reduce locking in strongly locked neurons [44]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Awake macaque single units [44,51,52]; ferret slice and simulation [37,53]; rat and human [54,55]
rows.what_is_missing: Whether human effects at 1–2 mA are direct [50,54]; a state-dependent dose rule [44]

rows.dose_quantities_reported: Only as part of a pooled tES safety envelope with tDCS and tACS: to 4 mA and 60 min/day, no serious adverse events over more than 300,000 sessions [43]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human safety pooling only [43]
rows.what_is_missing: Every mechanistic and dose-specific cell; absent from both comparison sources [30,31]

rows.drive_physically: Two kHz carriers at slightly different frequencies whose overlap produces a low-frequency amplitude envelope [39]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Envelope demodulation at the membrane: mouse neurons followed the envelope, hippocampal neurons were driven without driving overlying cortex, and motor responses were steered by current ratio [39]; in humans, modelled and cadaver-measured steering with changed hippocampal fMRI and improved episodic memory accuracy [45]
rows.named_rival: Passive membrane filtering cannot extract the envelope; ion-channel rectification can, and predicts tonic firing or conduction block in superficial tissue at intensities that reach deep targets (computational) [60]; modelled suprathreshold TI needs about 75–230 V/m against about 0.1–1 V/m attainable in the human brain [48]; in macaque, TI altered spike timing but not rate and was about 80% less potent than tACS [46]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Carrier frequency, difference frequency, per-channel current and current ratio [39]; human studies mostly used 20 Hz or gamma-range envelopes [47]
rows.resolution_reported: Steering claimed from models and cadaver measurements rather than from in vivo field recordings [45]; spike-timing effects without rate change in macaque [46]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human systematic review: 48 records, 20 completed studies and 28 ongoing trials, 820 participants, well tolerated, evidence at Phase 1 level with efficacy untested [47]; mouse [39]; macaque [46]; computational [48,60]
rows.what_is_missing: Efficacy of any kind [47]; adjudication of suprathreshold feasibility [46,48]; measured human in-brain envelope amplitude

rows.drive_physically: Current pulses delivered to the cervical vagus [140]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Recruitment of vagal afferents driving phasic locus coeruleus firing: rapid phasic bursts from 0.1 mA, with rate rising with current and pulse width, and pulse frequency shifting burst timing without changing total activity (rat) [140]
rows.named_rival: Not established in this corpus for the implanted route
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Current amplitude, pulse frequency, pulse width, train duration, inter-train interval [140]; effective dose often omitted in implantable practice [2]
rows.resolution_reported: Half-second trains produce phasic bursts in rat locus coeruleus; trigeminal pulse-locked activity appears only above 1.2 mA, giving an amplitude window that separates the two [140]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Rat direct recordings across a parameter grid [140]; clinical use as standard care [31]
rows.what_is_missing: Fibre-class selectivity: the vagus is a bundle of molecularly distinct afferent classes whose transduction is poorly established [157]; any human recording of the engaged pathway

rows.drive_physically: Current pulses at the auricular branch of the vagus [146]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Assumed to be the same afferent recruitment as cervical VNS [140]; in humans indexed only by proxies [146]
rows.named_rival: Null engagement: pooled continuous stimulation gives strong evidence for no pupil effect (g = 0.002, BF01 = 21.9) while pulsed stimulation gives strong evidence for one (g = 0.36, BF10 = 50.8) [146]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, and pulsed versus continuous delivery as the decisive parameter [146]
rows.resolution_reported: Not established in this corpus; the human read-out is a pupil proxy rather than a spatial or temporal measurement [146]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human living Bayesian meta-analysis, 18 studies, N = 771 [146]; rat parametric work by extension [140]
rows.what_is_missing: A direct human measure of target engagement; separation of vagal from trigeminal recruitment at the ear [140,157]

rows.dose_quantities_reported: Appears only as a recruitment control during VNS, where pulse-locked trigeminal activity appeared above 1.2 mA in rat [140]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Rat, as a control condition in a VNS parameter study [140]
rows.what_is_missing: Any source treating the trigeminal nerve as the intended target; it appears in neither cross-modality comparison source [30,31]

rows.invasiveness: Implanted nerve cuff with a respiration sensor; serious adverse events in under 2% [252]
rows.drive_physically: Current pulses to the hypoglossal nerve, gated to inspiration, producing timed tongue-protrusor contraction [252]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Excitation of a somatic motor nerve, with a mechanical endpoint (airway patency) rather than a modulated state [252]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Pulse width 90 against 120 µs and frequency 33 against 40 Hz, amplitude in volts, therapeutic window counted in tolerable voltage steps; the longer, faster configuration lowered the amplitude needed for functional protrusion across all three electrode configurations without changing the usable window [253]
rows.resolution_reported: Stimulation gated to the respiratory cycle, so the temporal unit is the breath [252]; no spatial figure in this corpus
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: 126 CPAP-intolerant patients, median apnoea–hypopnoea index down 68% from 29.3 to 9.0 events/hour at 12 months, with a randomised therapy-withdrawal substudy confirming device dependence [252]; pooled analysis of 30 studies (549 patients across 26 single-arm studies, 273 across 4 randomised trials), index down 20.11 events/hour (95% CI 23.13 to 17.10) at one year and 15.60 beyond [254]
rows.what_is_missing: Randomised evidence: only 4 of the 30 pooled studies were randomised [254]

rows.drive_physically: Current pulses to the occipital nerves, producing paraesthesia in the stimulated field [255]
rows.named_rival: Not established in this corpus; a 30% intensity arm matched the 100% arm, so a dose-dependent therapeutic effect cannot be separated from a non-specific one [255]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Intensity expressed as a percentage of the individually determined paraesthesia-to-near-discomfort range rather than in mA, set at 100% or 30% [255]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 3 dose-controlled trial in medically intractable chronic cluster headache, median weekly attack frequency falling substantially by weeks 21–24 (p < 0.0001), similarly in both arms [255]
rows.what_is_missing: A sham comparison, which an unmistakable paraesthesia makes impossible, and with it the mechanism of benefit [255]

rows.drive_physically: Current pulses in the epidural space over the spinal cord [2]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Recruitment of large myelinated dorsal-root afferents rather than motoneurons or interneurons directly, which then engage motor pools trans-synaptically; modelled and confirmed in rats for intensity and electrode position [61]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width, frequency, waveform; classification proposed by target plus waveform and dose, with effective dose often omitted [2]; charge-density and charge-per-phase limit by inheritance [17]
rows.resolution_reported: Recruitment order and threshold as a function of electrode position, modelled and rat-validated [61]; kHz waveforms optimised to inactivate sodium channels from the closed state can block conduction without an onset burst (computational) [62]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Computational model with rat validation [61,62]; expert consensus taxonomy [2]; clinical use [31]
rows.what_is_missing: Human mechanism data; frequency and duty-cycle terms in the safety rule [18]

rows.family: Peripheral nerve stimulation and functional electrical stimulation
rows.invasiveness: Surface electrodes through to fully implanted systems [245]
rows.drive_physically: Charge-balanced current pulses to intact peripheral motor nerves, with the safety envelope set by charge-injection limits rather than by seizure or cognitive risk [245]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Excitation of peripheral motor axons, with contraction graded by amplitude, pulse width and frequency [245]
rows.named_rival: Recruitment is non-selective, spatially fixed and temporally synchronous rather than following the size principle, and the textbook strict reverse (large-to-small) order is not supported; synchronous firing of the same units is the source of the rapid fatigue [246]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Amplitude, pulse width and frequency modulation as the grading variables [245]; the same peripheral drive alone reproduced tACS motor effects in rats and humans [54]; kHz waveforms optimised to inactivate sodium channels from the closed state block conduction without an onset burst (computational) [62]
rows.resolution_reported: Spatially fixed recruitment, so the stimulated population does not rotate as in voluntary contraction [246]; the outcome is a graded mechanical action rather than a modulated state [245]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: meta-analysis of 18 randomised trials after stroke, moderate pooled effect on activity driven mainly by upper-limb function with smaller gains in walking speed [247]; family review across upper and lower extremity, bladder, bowel and respiratory neuroprostheses [245]
rows.what_is_missing: A selective recruitment method that reproduces the size principle, and fatigue-resistant parameter sets [246]

rows.drive_physically: Focused pressure wave, pulsed, delivered through the skull [20]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Contested, with at least four candidates: intramembrane cavitation rectified into capacitance change (computational) [65]; mechanosensitive channels — TREK-1, TREK-2, TRAAK and NaV1.5 currents modulated by up to about 23% at 10 MHz and 0.3–4.9 W/cm² in oocytes [67], Piezo1 required in vivo in mouse cortex [68], astrocytic TRPA1 driving Best1 glutamate release onto neuronal NMDA receptors [69], and CFTR chloride flow at 0.8 MHz and 0.20 MPa in HEK cells [70]; acoustic radiation force, with responses growing from 0.5 to 43 MHz, which excludes cavitation in salamander retina [66]; and heating, where suppression tracked temperature and was independent of duty cycle, peak pressure and modulation frequency in rat thalamus [71]
rows.named_rival: Peripheral confound rather than direct coupling: guinea-pig activation was abolished by auditory-nerve transection or cochlear fluid removal [74], mouse cortical patterns matched the auditory pathway [75], and in humans the standard motor inhibition was driven by auditory stimulation across four experiments [77]; countered by intact motor responses in genetically deaf mice once pulse edges were smoothed [76]; scalp somatosensory sensation is a further route, driven by particle displacement [78]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Six reporting domains: transducer and drive system, drive settings, free-field acoustic parameters, pulse timing, in situ exposure estimates and intensity parameters [20]; mechanical index at or below 1.9 as non-significant risk plus three alternative thermal criteria, by the authors' statement expert opinion and not safety limits [19]; across 32 studies and 37 experiments, duty cycle (p = 0.046) and sonication duration (p = 0.04) predicted direction of effect while I<sub>SPPA</sub> alone did not (p = 0.256) [79]
rows.resolution_reported: Not established in this corpus as a measured human focal volume; in situ exposure is estimated rather than measured [20]; response duration tracked pulse duration in mouse [76]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human systematic review and meta-analysis, self-declared provisional [79]; human experiments [77,78]; rodent [68,71,74,75,76]; in vitro [66,67,70]; computational [65]
rows.what_is_missing: Which parameter sets the direction of effect [71,79]; complete parameter reporting [79]; the threshold for significant risk [19]

rows.invasiveness: Transcranial but tissue-destructive: an irreversible lesion without an incision [86]
rows.drive_physically: High-intensity focused ultrasound absorbed as heat at the focus [85]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Thermal coagulation, with dose expressed as cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C [85]
rows.named_rival: Not established in this corpus; the same physical modality is reversible at low intensity, so thermal dose rather than modality decides [85,86]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Temperature and thermal dose [85]; achievable peak temperature limited by skull density ratio (positive, p = 0.009) and skull volume (negative, p = 0.023) in 25 patients [87]
rows.resolution_reported: Lesion placed accurately enough to beat a sham procedure [86]; no millimetre figure in this corpus; effect is immediate and permanent [86]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised sham-controlled trial: hand tremor 18.1 to 9.6 at three months versus 16.0 to 15.8 with sham, gait disturbance in 36% and paraesthesia or numbness in 38% [86]; human retrospective series [87]
rows.what_is_missing: A per-patient account of skull transmission [87]; comparison against DBS on the same endpoints [31]

rows.drive_physically: Low-pressure focused ultrasound driving oscillation of circulating microbubbles at the vessel wall [80]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Microbubble cavitation at the endothelium rather than absorption in tissue, which is why it works far below ablative intensity [80]
rows.named_rival: Sterile inflammation as an intrinsic consequence: damage-associated molecular patterns and a parenchymal inflammatory response lasting about 24 h, compared by the authors to ischaemia or mild traumatic brain injury (rat) [83]; against microbubble dose as the controlling variable, with no significant NF-κB change at clinical imaging doses and oedema, degeneration and microhaemorrhage at high doses (rat) [84]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Temporal peak acoustic power 0.2–11.5 W in rabbit [80]; 0.28 ± 0.05 MPa mean peak pressure at 551.5 kHz, 10 ms bursts, 2 Hz PRF, held at a fraction of the ultraharmonic-emission threshold, with opening and no detectable damage at 50% scaling [81]; microbubble dose [84]
rows.resolution_reported: Opening confined to the targeted volume and imageable by contrast-enhanced MR, reversible and repeatable [80,82]; enhancement scaled linearly with the chosen pressure fraction [81]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Rabbit [80] and rat [81,83,84]; human phase I in five patients with Alzheimer's disease, safe and reversible with no group-level amyloid change [82]
rows.what_is_missing: Therapeutic benefit as distinct from barrier opening [82]; an agreed inflammatory threshold [83,84]

rows.invasiveness: Non-invasive and neuronavigated, with high tolerability and no serious adverse events reported [228]
rows.drive_physically: Single ultrashort ultrasound shockwave pulses of roughly 3 µs rather than a continuous or tone-burst beam, so the drive has essentially no duty cycle [228]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Not established in this corpus: the introductory paper lists candidates — transient membrane pore formation, neurotransmitter and neurotrophin changes, microglial activation, nitric oxide signalling — without establishing one [228]; in mice, clinical-range energy produced calcium influx, raised c-Fos in dentate gyrus and transiently reorganised limbic network connectivity, reverting within about ten minutes [230]
rows.named_rival: A second mechanism appears at a modest energy increase: 0.25 mJ/mm² triggered spreading depolarisation waves where 0.05 mJ/mm² produced the direct activation pattern (mouse) [230]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Energy flux density 0.2–0.3 mJ/mm², about 3 µs per pulse, 5 Hz, about 6,000 pulses per session, with measured temporal-peak intensity falling roughly 80–90% through human skull [228]; the randomised trial used 6,000 pulses at 0.20 mJ/mm² and 5 Hz [229]
rows.resolution_reported: Neuronavigated focal delivery [228]; mouse network changes reverting to baseline within about ten minutes [230]; no measured human focal volume
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: the sham-controlled primary endpoint was negative — in a double-blind crossover trial in 60 patients on standard therapy, CERAD corrected total score rose 2.22 points after verum against 1.00 after sham at three months, but the condition-by-session interaction was not significant (P = .68), with benefit only in a prespecified subgroup aged 70 or under and successful blinding [229]; the 35-patient open-label series it supersedes reported three-month improvement correlated with memory-network connectivity [228]; mouse imaging [230]
rows.what_is_missing: A confirmed clinical effect, since the sham-controlled trial does not reproduce the open-label result [228,229]; an established coupling mechanism [228,230]

rows.invasiveness: Fully non-invasive, with no adverse clinical or laboratory effects in the first human study [256,259]
rows.drive_physically: Focused ultrasound aimed at a sub-organ visceral target — splenic, hepatic or hepatoportal — rather than at a nerve trunk or the brain [256]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Mechanical activation of nerve terminals inside the organ with afferent relay to brain: splenic stimulation engaged the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway comparably with surgical VNS and hepatic stimulation altered glucose regulation, with imaging showing engagement of metabolism-related brain regions [256]; the hepatoportal effect required an intact liver-to-brain pathway, verified by denervation, in mice, rats and swine [258]
rows.named_rival: A local tissue effect rather than a neural reflex [256]; in humans the effect did not differ by stimulation mode or across a roughly fifteen-fold intensity difference, which is hard to reconcile with a dose-dependent mechanical-neural mechanism [259]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Human: three minutes delivered in intermittent 15 s intervals, either swept continuously at 11.7 mW/cm² or focused-pulsed at 174.8–225.4 mW/cm² [259]; in mice the benefit depended on specific stimulation parameters [257]
rows.resolution_reported: Sub-organ targeting rather than focality in neural tissue [256]; in humans, ex vivo TNF production fell for more than two hours and returned to baseline by 24 h [259]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human first-in-human study in healthy volunteers [259]; rodent work from two independent groups [256,257], with single-cell RNA sequencing implicating T and B cell populations [257]; cross-species to swine [258]
rows.what_is_missing: Any human measurement of the neurotransmitter relay, which remains inferred from the preclinical work, and any energy–response relationship [259]

rows.drive_physically: Red to near-infrared light applied at the scalp, for example an 810 nm LED helmet or a 905 nm laser [22]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Cytochrome c oxidase as photoacceptor, argued from competition with potassium cyanide and from efficacy tracking the enzyme's absorption spectrum, with 670 and 830 nm effective and 728 nm not; cell death fell from 83.6% to 43.5% at 300 µM KCN in primary neurons [88]; nitric oxide photodissociation as the signalling step [89]
rows.named_rival: Insufficient delivered dose: more than 99% of light absorbed or scattered by human skull, maximum transmittance 0.31% for a 905 nm laser and 0.71% for an 810 nm LED helmet, with mitochondrial responses appearing only 14–775 times above the transmitted level [22]; against Monte Carlo simulation putting up to about 15% of incident energy at cortex transcranially and about 1% intranasally, reduced by melanin [23]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Wavelength, irradiance in mW/cm², fluence in J/cm², with a claimed biphasic dose response in which low fluence stimulates more than high [21]
rows.resolution_reported: Deposition concentrated in ventromedial prefrontal cortex in simulation [23]; no measured focal volume or time constant in this corpus
rows.dominant_evidence_base: In vitro primary neurons and HeLa cells [88,89]; human skull specimens with in vitro dose comparison [22]; photon-transport simulation [23]; proponent review [21]
rows.what_is_missing: Agreement on the fraction of light reaching cortex [22,23]; skin pigmentation as a reported covariate [23]; any dose standard [21]

rows.drive_physically: A molecule delivered to plasma and distributed by blood flow and barrier transport [164]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Ligand binding at a receptor, described by affinity, occupancy and efficacy in the operational model [91], with exposure at the target site, target binding and expression of pharmacological activity as the three steps that have to be shown separately [24]; for neurosteroids, positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A rather than agonism [179]
rows.named_rival: The coupling step can be membrane-biophysical rather than a lock-and-key receptor event, with anaesthetic-sensitive sites in ordered lipid domains [184]; and receptor location can decide the effect, since psychedelic plasticity requires intracellular rather than surface 5-HT2A receptors [92]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Ketamine 0.5 mg/kg as a single infusion, with improvement at 110 min, response 71% and remission 29% at day 1 (n = 18, crossover) [166]; brexanolone as a single 60 h titrated infusion, Hamilton reduction 14.6 versus 12.1 points at 60 h [180]; occupancy as a dose proxy, 38–87% D2 predicting response with thresholds near 65% for response, 72% for extrapyramidal symptoms and 78% for hyperprolactinaemia [26], and windows of 65–80% D2 and 70–80% SERT [27]; plasma exposure as AUC and C<sub>max</sub> [25]
rows.resolution_reported: Spatial selectivity comes from receptor distribution and barrier transport, not from delivery [164]; temporal profile is pharmacokinetic, and the ketamine effect outlasted clearance by about a week [166]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised trials [166,180]; human PET [26,27]; systematic review of 110 studies and 37,193 participants [28]
rows.what_is_missing: Measured target-site concentration rather than modelled [164]; an efficacy term alongside occupancy, since partial agonists keep extrapyramidal risk low at high occupancy [28]

rows.drive_physically: A molecule absorbed from the gut into plasma [186]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: As intravenous: receptor binding and occupancy [91]
rows.named_rival: As intravenous [184,92]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Zuranolone 50 mg once daily for 14 days, Hamilton-17 least-squares mean difference −4.0 (95% CI −6.3 to −1.7), n = 196 [181]; levodopa dosing complicated by erratic plasma uptake and large dose-to-dose variability [186]
rows.resolution_reported: Temporal profile imposed by absorption: pulsatile versus continuous exposure of the same receptors gives different long-term outcomes [186]; no spatial selectivity beyond receptor distribution [164]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 3 trial [181]; clinical pharmacology review [186]
rows.what_is_missing: Delivery consistency rather than receptor pharmacology as the limiting factor [186]; whether these agents outperform existing treatments, judged insufficient by one review [181]

rows.drive_physically: A molecule deposited on nasal mucosa [161]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Direct nose-to-brain transport along olfactory and trigeminal pathways by perineural and perivascular bulk flow [161]
rows.named_rival: Systemic absorption rather than direct transport; the pharmacokinetic evidence for a direct human route is contested [161]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Flexibly dosed intranasal esketamine added to a newly started oral antidepressant, n = 227, greater MADRS improvement by day 28, with dissociation, nausea, vertigo, dysgeusia and dizziness generally resolving within about 1.5 h [169]
rows.resolution_reported: Simulation of intranasal light puts about 1% of energy at cortex, which is the nearest analogue in this corpus rather than a drug measurement [23]; no measured human nose-to-brain distribution
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 3 registration trial [169]; mechanism review, mixed species [161]
rows.what_is_missing: Quantification of the direct fraction in humans [161]; blinding, since dissociative effects are unmasking [169]

rows.drive_physically: A gas taken up across the alveolar membrane [185]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Anaesthetic action at sites inside ion channels and within the plasma membrane [184]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Nitrous oxide, one-hour inhalations at 25% or 50%, n = 24 crossover: improvement versus placebo (P = 0.01), no difference between concentrations (P = 0.58), adverse events far fewer at 25% (P < 0.001) [185]
rows.resolution_reported: Separation from placebo emerged at weeks 1 and 2 rather than at 2 or 24 hours, so the outcome outlasts exposure by weeks [185]; no spatial selectivity reported
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human phase 2 crossover trial [185]; in vitro mechanism review [184]
rows.what_is_missing: Dose–response for efficacy, which saturated while side effects remained dose-dependent [185]

rows.drive_physically: A molecule infused into the cerebrospinal fluid compartment [163]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Receptor occupancy placed at the spinal cord rather than the brain: GABA-B agonism where the circuit is, not where the side effects are [163]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Continuous pump infusion of baclofen: tone fell in all 20 patients and spasms were reduced in 18 of 19, maintained over a mean 19.2 months, in patients who had failed the oral route [163]
rows.resolution_reported: Compartment-level rather than focal selectivity; continuous rather than pulsed delivery [163]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human randomised double-blind crossover trial, n = 20 [163]
rows.what_is_missing: Target-site concentration measurement [164]; comparison with implanted stimulation on the same endpoint [2]

rows.drive_physically: A sustained pressure gradient driving bulk flow of infusate through the extracellular space [160]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Convective transport replacing diffusion, so distribution is set by infusion physics rather than by molecular diffusivity [160]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Infusion rate, volume, catheter placement and tissue hydraulic conductivity; distribution-to-infusion volume about 6:1 for ¹¹¹In-transferrin and about 13:1 for ¹⁴C-sucrose, with local concentrations orders of magnitude above achievable systemic levels [160]
rows.resolution_reported: Centimetres of spread rather than millimetres, with the large molecule more uniformly distributed at 24 h [160]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Mixed-species intraparenchymal infusion experiments [160]
rows.what_is_missing: Human outcome data in this corpus; comparison with FUS barrier opening as the other route for large molecules [80,160]

rows.invasiveness: Non-invasive and home-delivered, with adherence of 85–90% and no serious treatment-related adverse events over six months [234]
rows.drive_physically: Patterned light and sound delivered to the sense organs at a chosen frequency [231]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Sensory transduction into a rhythmic cortical response whose amplitude is resonant rather than flat: human EEG stepped across 1–100 Hz flicker showed peaks near 10, 20, 40 and 80 Hz [231]
rows.named_rival: Linear superposition rather than entrainment: steady-state responses were reproduced by shifting and summing rate-matched transient evoked responses, with no signature of oscillatory entrainment at the stimulation frequency (human) [232]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Frequency as the dose axis, with measured resonance peaks [231]; 40 Hz combined light and sound, one hour daily for three months [233]; EEG-verified 40 Hz audio-visual delivery over six months [234]
rows.resolution_reported: Frequency specificity in the driven response [231]; delivery is whole-pathway rather than focal, since selectivity comes from the sense organ and not from a field [231,232]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: the largest sham-controlled trial missed its primary cognitive composite in 70 analysable patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease randomised 2:1, with nominally favourable unadjusted secondaries — MMSE decline reduced 76%, ADCS-ADL decline 77%, whole-brain volume loss 69% [234]; pilot work showed tolerability and reliable EEG entrainment, and in 15 patients less ventricular dilation and hippocampal atrophy [233]; human EEG mechanism studies [231,232]
rows.what_is_missing: Whether the driven response involves an entrained oscillator at all [231,232]; a positive primary endpoint [234]; multiplicity-adjusted secondary outcomes [234]

rows.invasiveness: Non-invasive transmastoid electrodes, described as simple and safe [235]
rows.drive_physically: Direct or alternating current passed between mastoid electrodes into the vestibular periphery [235]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: DC bias of firing in vestibular primary afferents at the spike-initiation zone rather than at the hair cell or the central nuclei, with irregular afferents most sensitive; the vector of biased signals converging in the vestibular nuclei predicts the direction and size of body sway across montages [235]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Current amplitude 0.1–4 mA, session duration 12 s to 24 h, and direct, sinusoidal or stochastic waveforms, extracted from 53 clinical trials, some parameters near-standard within an indication and others with no convention [237]
rows.resolution_reported: Organ-level selectivity set by montage and polarity rather than by focality of the field [235]; evokes eye movements and postural responses without head motion, so vestibular processing can be dissociated from actual acceleration [236]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: review-level forward model from montage to sway [235]; systematic parameter review across 53 clinical trials in vestibular loss, cerebellar ataxia, Parkinson's disease, post-stroke neglect, motion sickness and balance impairment [237]; cross-species mechanism review [236]
rows.what_is_missing: Parameter consensus across indications, and pooled efficacy estimates by indication [237]

rows.drive_physically: A constant magnetic field held over the scalp, with no time variation and therefore no induced electric field [238]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Not established in this corpus: no accepted transduction pathway exists for a static field, and the reported excitability change was localised to intracortical rather than peripheral or spinal mechanisms by control conditions [238]
rows.named_rival: Non-replication: ten minutes at matched magnet geometry produced no MEP modulation in 18 subjects, with or without a concurrent attentional task [240]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Flux density at cortex, about 160–170 mT at 2 cm from the scalp for a 45 × 30 mm N45 magnet and about 160–245 mT for N52 magnets, with protocols of 5–15 min, 20–30 min or two hours, up to three daily sessions [241]
rows.resolution_reported: Focality set by magnet geometry, with effects reported as site-dependent across motor, somatosensory and visual cortex, cerebellum and spinal cord [239]; after-effects outlasting a ten-minute application by several minutes [238]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: single-session excitability studies, with MEP amplitude reduced by up to about 25% after ten minutes [238]; qualitative pooling of 27 studies, predominantly inhibitory, with no aggregated effect sizes [239]; four randomised clinical trials, including 50 patients with levodopa-induced dyskinesia and a phase 2 ALS trial with no short-term functional difference but a 73% lower risk of death or tracheostomy at 18 months [241]
rows.what_is_missing: A pooled effect-size estimate, so the effect size rests on single studies [239]; replication of the excitability effect [238,240]; any transduction mechanism [238]

rows.invasiveness: Implanted or intraoperative surface device; cooling produced no appreciable cortical damage even at low temperatures [242]
rows.drive_physically: Heat extraction from tissue, delivered in preclinical work by thermoelectric (Peltier) devices [242]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Temperature dependence of channel kinetics and synaptic release, so the drive slows every temperature-dependent conductance and release step at once [242]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Target temperature: about 20 °C terminates paroxysmal activity in vitro and below 24 °C aborts seizures within seconds in vivo [242]; cooling a songbird premotor nucleus slowed song by up to 45% while leaving acoustic structure intact, graded with temperature [244]; achieved human cortical cooling was only about 0.6–2 °C at 10–15 mm depth [243]
rows.resolution_reported: Region-specific and graded, present only while cooled: cooling one nucleus changed behavioural tempo while cooling the downstream nucleus did not [244]; thermal penetration limited to the first 10–15 mm from the human cortical surface [243]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Preclinical: in vitro and in vivo seizure work, reviewed [242]; songbird causal manipulation [244]; human and canine intraoperative thermometry [243]
rows.what_is_missing: The gap between species: the 20–24 °C that works preclinically [242] cannot currently be delivered at depth in human cortex, where surface cooling achieved 0.6–2 °C [243]; any human therapeutic series

rows.invasiveness: Implanted penetrating arrays in participants who also carry recording arrays [250]
rows.drive_physically: Charge injection through array electrodes used as an input channel alongside neural recording [248]
rows.proposed_primary_coupling: Direct cortical excitation writing contact location and pressure information into somatosensory cortex for closed-loop prosthetic control [248]
rows.dose_quantities_reported: Per-electrode amplitude, with detection thresholds of a median 31.5 µA at day 100 falling to 10.4 µA at day 1500 [250]; amplitude and frequency set the modality of the percept as well as its magnitude [249]
rows.resolution_reported: Single-electrode write-in, with percepts stable over months [248]; stimulated arrays retained signal amplitude better than unstimulated ones over 1,500 days [250]
rows.dominant_evidence_base: Human: single-participant implanted series [248,249,250] and a six-month 96-channel visual cortex implant [251]; the corpus's other closed-loop exemplars gate a fixed drive on a measured signal rather than writing in — biomarker-gated DBS [135] and cavitation-feedback ultrasound [81]
rows.what_is_missing: Performance of a full decode-and-write-in loop as a system, and any multi-participant series [248,250]

label: Figure 7
title: The dispute map: 23 live disagreements and their rival positions
caption: One node per dispute from section 14, each linked to the rival positions named there, with the species and evidence kind of each position on its own node. Each dispute carries a property saying whether the split is about mechanism (12), dose (7) or endpoint (4). Most disputes have two positions; the ultrasound transducer, the tDCS after-effect, ketamine's active species, 5-HT2A necessity and transcutaneous vagal engagement have three or four.
how_to_read: Pick a dispute node and read its question, then read each position hanging off it as a claim with its own preparation attached. Use the split property to set your expectations: a dose split can often be closed by reporting parameters, while a mechanism split usually needs a new experiment, and an endpoint split means the two sides measured different things. In almost none of these is one side simply wrong, so read the pair as two claims measured differently rather than as a right answer and a wrong one. The identifiers on the dispute nodes are the ones the graph will carry, so you can follow any of them back to its entry in section 14.
source: Built from section 14 of the review, one dispute node per numbered entry (14.1 to 14.23) and one position node per position that section names, with each position's species and evidence kind taken from the same entry. The mechanism/dose/endpoint classification is this volume's, assigned from what each entry says the evidence turns on; several entries could be read either way, and the ones the prose itself resolves into dose rather than mechanism are marked dose. Position wording is compressed from the entries and carries their reference numbers; nothing is quantitative.

nodes.label: 14.1 Transcranial field entrainment
nodes.question: Do 1-2 mA transcranial currents modulate cortical neurons directly?

nodes.label: Direct cortical entrainment
nodes.detail: tACS entrained weakly locked macaque units and desynchronised strongly locked ones, and did so through topical scalp anaesthesia

nodes.label: Peripheral, or too weak
nodes.detail: rat recordings put the minimum effective field near 1 mV/mm, and skin anaesthesia removed tACS tremor entrainment that peripheral nerve stimulation reproduced

nodes.label: 14.2 Temporal interference thresholds in humans
nodes.question: Does temporal interference reach neural thresholds in the human brain?

nodes.label: Envelope neuromodulation
nodes.detail: anaesthetised mice followed the envelope, and human TI changed hippocampal fMRI activity and memory accuracy

nodes.label: Unreachable in a human head
nodes.detail: modelled suprathreshold TI needs about 75-230 V/m against 0.1-1 V/m delivered, and passive filtering cannot demodulate the envelope

nodes.label: 14.3 The ultrasound transducer
nodes.question: What converts a pressure wave into a change in neural activity?

nodes.label: Intramembrane cavitation
nodes.detail: leaflets separate under acoustic drive, rectifying pressure into a capacitance change

nodes.label: Acoustic radiation force
nodes.detail: retinal responses grew from 0.5 to 43 MHz, opposite to the cavitation prediction

nodes.label: Mechanosensitive channels
nodes.detail: Piezo1 knockout cut evoked calcium and EMG; CFTR carried ultrasound-evoked chloride current

nodes.label: Heat
nodes.detail: rat thalamic suppression tracked temperature, not duty cycle

nodes.label: 14.4 The ultrasound auditory confound
nodes.question: Are reported ultrasound effects produced at the focus or through the ear?

nodes.label: Auditory-driven
nodes.detail: activation abolished by auditory nerve transection, mouse imaging matched the auditory pathway, and human motor inhibition tracked auditory stimulation

nodes.label: Genuine at the focus
nodes.detail: envelope smoothing removed the auditory brainstem response but left the mouse motor response intact, and deaf mice matched hearing ones

nodes.label: 14.5 Barrier opening and sterile inflammation
nodes.question: Is focused-ultrasound blood-brain-barrier opening an inflammatory injury?

nodes.label: An inflammatory event
nodes.detail: damage-associated molecular patterns and a parenchymal sterile inflammatory response lasting about 24 hours

nodes.label: A dose effect
nodes.detail: NF-kB activation tracked microbubble dose, absent at clinical imaging doses

nodes.label: 14.6 Photobiomodulation delivered dose
nodes.question: Does enough near-infrared light reach cortex for transcranial photobiomodulation?

nodes.label: Insufficient
nodes.detail: maximum transmittance through human skull 0.31-0.71%, with cell responses needing 14-775 times that level

nodes.label: Sufficient
nodes.detail: Monte Carlo photon transport put up to about 15% of incident energy at cortex

nodes.label: 14.7 40 Hz sensory stimulation
nodes.question: Does 40 Hz sensory stimulation entrain gamma and reduce amyloid?

nodes.label: Yes
nodes.detail: optogenetic 40 Hz lowered amyloid, and audiovisual 40 Hz raised CSF influx with clearance-dependent amyloid removal

nodes.label: No
nodes.detail: large-scale recordings found no native gamma engagement, flicker avoidance and no plaque change

nodes.label: 14.8 The tDCS after-effect account
nodes.question: Is the after-effect of tDCS cortical LTP-like plasticity?

nodes.label: LTP-like plasticity
nodes.detail: sustained MEP change read as associative plasticity, as in paired associative stimulation

nodes.label: Peripheral co-stimulation
nodes.detail: six tDCS results re-read as cranial and cervical nerve co-stimulation

nodes.label: Unreliable
nodes.detail: 430 participants across 22 theta-burst studies varied widely, and 59 studies found no single-session cognitive effect

nodes.label: Glial
nodes.detail: the effect required astrocytic calcium

nodes.label: 14.9 Connectivity-based targeting
nodes.question: Does subgenual cingulate connectivity predict rTMS outcome well enough to target by?

nodes.label: Yes
nodes.detail: across 98 healthy subjects, sites with better reported efficacy were more strongly anticorrelated with subgenual cingulate

nodes.label: Too weak to target by
nodes.detail: in 295 treated patients the association was about r = -0.16, some 3% of outcome variance

nodes.label: 14.10 Deep brain stimulation mechanism
nodes.question: How does high-frequency deep brain stimulation produce a lesion-like effect?

nodes.label: Informational lesion
nodes.detail: modelled high-frequency drive makes output spiking regular and almost variance-free

nodes.label: Excitation and antidromic activation
nodes.detail: high-frequency stimulation drives efferent axons rather than silencing them

nodes.label: 14.11 The charge-density safety rule
nodes.question: Does the charge and charge-density rule bound safe stimulation?

nodes.label: The Shannon line
nodes.detail: a log-linear boundary fitted to tissue-damage data became the design rule for macroelectrodes

nodes.label: Out of scope
nodes.detail: the equation omits frequency, duty cycle, current density and electrode size, and microelectrodes deliver more charge without damage

nodes.label: 14.12 The inflammatory-reflex framing
nodes.question: Is vagal control of splenic TNF a reflex arc, or a drivable pathway?

nodes.label: A reflex
nodes.detail: a hard-wired loop with afferent limb, central integration and efferent cholinergic limb, with ChAT-expressing splenic T cells completing the arc

nodes.label: Drivable but not a reflex
nodes.detail: the disynaptic vagus-to-splenic-nerve link is rejected, since vagal stimulation drives no splenic nerve spikes

nodes.label: 14.13 Transcutaneous vagal target engagement
nodes.question: Does transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation engage noradrenergic targets in humans?

nodes.label: Null
nodes.detail: continuous cymba conchae stimulation in 66 participants left pupil, cortisol and cardiac vagal activity unchanged

nodes.label: Protocol-dependent
nodes.detail: pulsed delivery gave an effect (g = 0.36) and continuous delivery evidence for the null (g = 0.002)

nodes.label: Weak proxy
nodes.detail: locus coeruleus recording with pupillometry gave a variable, state-dependent mapping

nodes.label: 14.14 Ketamine's active species
nodes.question: Is (2R,6R)-hydroxynorketamine the antidepressant species, and does it have a target?

nodes.label: Yes, without NMDA inhibition
nodes.detail: the metabolite acted without NMDA receptor inhibition and required AMPA receptor activation

nodes.label: No target found
nodes.detail: screens across thousands of human proteins found no direct interaction with any proposed target

nodes.label: A shared downstream step
nodes.detail: NMDA antagonist pretreatment abolished the effects of ketamine, the metabolite and two unrelated compounds alike; an earlier account routes it through eEF2 kinase

nodes.label: 14.15 5-HT2A necessity
nodes.question: Is postsynaptic 5-HT2A signalling necessary for psychedelic-induced plasticity?

nodes.label: Postsynaptic 5-HT2A
nodes.detail: the standard account, with the hallucinogenic and the plasticity question separated

nodes.label: Presynaptic and afferent
nodes.detail: strengthening occurred where postsynaptic 5-HT2A is absent and needed presynaptic 5-HT2A on thalamic axons

nodes.label: TrkB rather than 5-HT2A
nodes.detail: plasticity required TrkB, not 5-HT2A, while head-twitch required 5-HT2A

nodes.label: 14.16 The subjective-experience question
nodes.question: Is the subjective experience necessary for a psychedelic's enduring therapeutic effect?

nodes.label: Necessary
nodes.detail: with drug intensity controlled, specific subjective features predict outcome across human studies

nodes.label: Not necessary
nodes.detail: the experience-to-outcome link is largely correlational, and lasting changes can occur without it

nodes.label: 14.17 Ketamine versus ECT
nodes.question: Is ketamine non-inferior to electroconvulsive therapy for depression?

nodes.label: Inferior for remission
nodes.detail: remission 63% with ECT against 46% with ketamine in hospitalised patients, so non-inferiority failed

nodes.label: Non-inferior for response
nodes.detail: response 55.4% with ketamine against 41.2% with ECT in 403 outpatients, meeting non-inferiority

nodes.label: 14.18 Intranasal direct transport
nodes.question: Does intranasal dosing reach the brain other than through systemic absorption?

nodes.label: Yes, an anatomical route
nodes.detail: olfactory and trigeminal pathways with perineural and perivascular bulk flow

nodes.label: Not shown quantitatively
nodes.detail: of about 100 studies, twelve met pharmacokinetic criteria and two rat studies supported direct transport, with no human evidence

nodes.label: 14.19 Receptor-occupancy thresholds
nodes.question: Is there a universal receptor-occupancy therapeutic window?

nodes.label: A threshold
nodes.detail: raclopride PET put occupancy at 38-87%, with response, extrapyramidal symptoms and hyperprolactinaemia likelier above about 65, 72 and 78%

nodes.label: It breaks for partial agonists
nodes.detail: in 110 studies and 37,193 participants, extrapyramidal risk rose above 75-85% occupancy for antagonists while partial agonists kept it low

nodes.label: 14.20 The serotonin premise
nodes.question: Does the serotonin-deficit premise behind serotonergic antidepressants hold?

nodes.label: No deficit evidence
nodes.detail: no association between serotonin metabolites and depression, and no genotype-by-stress interaction in the largest studies

nodes.label: Function-based, no deficit required
nodes.detail: the action sits in early changes to emotional and social information processing and in drug-induced plasticity

nodes.label: 14.21 The origin of the TMS-evoked potential
nodes.question: How much of the TMS-evoked EEG potential is transcranial rather than sensory?

nodes.label: Largely sensory
nodes.detail: a realistic sham reproducing auditory and somatosensory effects evoked responses resembling real TMS, early and late

nodes.label: Separable
nodes.detail: an optimised sham left early components and beta responses only with real TMS

nodes.label: 14.22 Magnetogenetics
nodes.question: Can magnetic fields gate ferritin-tethered ion channels as reported?

nodes.label: Yes, as reported
nodes.detail: a TRPV4-ferritin fusion permitted magnetic control in imaging, slice and in vivo electrophysiology and behaviour

nodes.label: Physically impossible
nodes.detail: required forces, torques and heating exceed what paramagnetic ferritin can supply by five to ten orders of magnitude

nodes.label: 14.23 The chemogenetic actuator
nodes.question: Is clozapine-N-oxide inert at targets other than the designer receptor?

nodes.label: Inert by design
nodes.detail: designer receptors activated by clozapine-N-oxide and not acetylcholine, with a Gi-coupled member silencing hippocampal neurons

nodes.label: Acting through clozapine
nodes.detail: the injected compound does not enter the brain and binds weakly; it is converted to clozapine, which enters and occupies the receptor

label: Figure 9
title: The proposed starter schema: node types, predicates and their ontology anchors
caption: The starter schema of section 15 drawn as a graph: node types as nodes, each carrying the ontology that anchors it, and the main predicates as edges, each carrying the properties that must travel with it. Ten of the seventeen node types are marked unanchored, including the two the section says have no ontology at all - the stimulation protocol, which has to be authored, and outcome measures - together with the protein slot inside the transducer and receptor nodes, the hypothesis group and the path. The claim edge appears as a node because confounds, hypothesis groups and paths attach to claim edges rather than to entities.
how_to_read: Read each node as a type, not an instance: "transducer" is the class that cytochrome c oxidase or Piezo1 would be an instance of. The anchor tells you which ontology supplies identifiers for that type; where the node is marked unanchored, you would have to author the vocabulary yourself, and the section says as much. Read each edge label as the predicate and the property list as what an import would reject the edge for missing. Take the whole figure as a starting point offered for redesign, not as a specification.
source: Built from section 15 of the review: the node types, anchors and predicates are the rows of the table in section 15.5, and the required edge properties are that table's fourth column. Three nodes not named as rows in the table are added so that every predicate has a defined endpoint - compartment and receptor, which the drug-drive row's predicates point at, and claim edge, which the confound, hypothesis-group and path rows point at - each anchored from the same section's text. The plasticity-state and circuit-state nodes come from the predicates in their rows. Where the section gives a predicate without fixing its range, the edge notes say so. Nothing is quantitative, and the schema is a proposal, not a standard.

nodes.label: Drive, nominal
nodes.note: Parameter set with units and not-reported markers; no ontology in the corpus covers stimulation protocols or device parameters [79,193].

nodes.label: Delivered quantity, effective
nodes.note: Measured or modelled, orientation, neural element, unit and species travel with the edge [79].

nodes.label: Drug drive
nodes.note: Route, schedule, exposure measure, active species and compartment reached are properties, not annotations [29,92].

nodes.label: Transducer
nodes.anchor: Cell Ontology [215]; GO cellular component [216]; protein slot open
nodes.note: The protein slot is named but unanchored: the corpus holds no reference describing a protein ontology [215,216,217].

nodes.label: Compartment
nodes.note: Receptor compartment is an attribute of the coupling node, because the same agonist acts differently inside the cell and at the surface [92].

nodes.label: Receptor
nodes.note: Affinity, occupancy, efficacy, the operational model, allosteric and ligand-selective states are settled as concepts, not as identifiers [91].

nodes.label: Cell population
nodes.anchor: Cell Ontology [215]; Neuron Phenotype Ontology for neurons [156]
nodes.note: Neuron types are decomposed into phenotypes rather than named as classes [156].

nodes.label: Plasticity state
nodes.note: Carries protocol, readout, preparation and responder fraction; direction is a distribution over participants, not a sign.

nodes.label: Molecular endpoint
nodes.note: Carries assay, preparation, direction and a one-laboratory flag, or incoming edges are not comparable [118,216].

nodes.label: Circuit / target
nodes.note: Anatomical, functional and connectivity-derived targets are different nodes [131].

nodes.label: Circuit state
nodes.note: Brain state and biomarker travel with the modulating edge, with the perturbation method named [131,139].

nodes.label: Body-system node, including non-neuronal relays
nodes.note: Admits non-neuronal relays: ChAT-expressing T cells and epithelial sensor cells [150,158].

nodes.label: Outcome measures
nodes.note: Unanchored: no ontology in this corpus covers outcome measures; the node carries effect size as reported, population and comparator.

nodes.label: Confound
nodes.note: Controls applied, blinding check and engagement shown; a confound is a node with edges to the claims it threatens [79].

nodes.label: Hypothesis group
nodes.note: Holds rival claim edges together with the discriminating experiment.

nodes.label: Path
nodes.note: Ordered claim edges, recording species changes and the weakest link; mechanism is a path, not an edge [223].

nodes.label: Claim edge
nodes.anchor: ECO for evidence type [218]; GRADE for certainty [208]
nodes.note: Every claim edge carries evidence type, certainty, species and preparation, and a link to its source, plus the dose and state that qualify its sign; an edge without these is not importable [155,208,218].
